summary.intent: Work through the NEXT-WORK plan for the Callisto release tool (SYS-RETRY fix, test debt, docs refresh, init/derive refactors, SYS-NAPI), then optimize the critical path performance, including whether to replace system git with gix or another library, and ideas like git hooks and ref metadata.
summary.outcome: Opened many PRs (#202-#208 for plan lanes, #327/#328/#330 stacked perf PRs, plus a parallel-history PR) with `just ci` passing. Measured gix and git2 against system git and kept the git binary, because gix is 3-10x slower on deep history at large scale. Closed the mistaken plan PR #201 and kept the plan local.

repo: Tracking and handoff plans such as NEXT-WORK.md must stay local (`.claude/plans/`, excluded via `.git/info/exclude`) and never go in a PR.
`just ci` is the gate (coverage threshold 90%); the wrapper script's exit code is not the verdict, so read the log's own `exit=` line.
The sandbox rejects inline `env` commands, heredocs, and scripts mentioning `git`, so scripts go in files via the Write tool, and edits are only allowed inside the current worktree.
macOS bash lacks `mapfile`, so generated workflow templates must use portable loops.
Release harness fakes (gh, cargo, registry) can hide bugs; black-box tests with the real binary and real jq are preferred (e.g. generated_workflow_napi_roster_tests.rs).
Commits and PRs must not include session links, per AGENTS.md; ADR changes (e.g. superseding ADR 5) require user acceptance.
Native stacks are linked with `gh stack` (e.g. #207 holds #205, #206, #208; #329 holds #327, #328, #330).

Benchmark fixtures must tag packages independently across history; tagging all packages on one commit hid a 500-process `git log` problem (status at 500 packages was 11.7 s vs 206 ms after the single-pass fix).
Intent JSON omits `artifactSlots` when empty, so jq `.artifactSlots[]` iterates null in generated workflows.

code.finding: GitAccess uses the system git binary, so there is no gix cache to tune in production code today.

changed_since_last_tag now uses a single `git log` pass with a symmetric-difference rule (a commit counts if reachable from HEAD or the tag but not both), verified equivalent to the old per-tag walk across merge and unmerged-hotfix topologies.

Local release selection now observes releases already tagged at HEAD across all providers, so a rerun after a failed tag push completes; a tag on an older commit still settles without provider contact.
Tag type check reads only the object type, so signed or multi-paragraph tag messages are no longer rejected.

workflow: Write the failing reproduction first, and mutation-test new tests (revert or break the source to confirm they fail).
For refactors, commit snapshot/characterization tests on unchanged code first, then do moves-only commits with the snapshots passing unchanged.
Measure before swapping libraries: spikes showed gix 3-10x slower than git log at large history, and the first profile and benchmarks were misleading until the fixture was made realistic.
Retract earlier claims when measurement contradicts them (the 2 GB cache speedup was warm second-pass reuse; the 5x commit-hash batch claim measured about 25%).
Stack dependent PRs and run just ci one at a time, since the cargo lock is shared; use a separate target dir for profiling builds.

friction: PR #201 wrongly put the local plan file in a PR and had to be closed.
Sandbox restrictions on heredocs, inline env, and compound commands forced script-file workarounds repeatedly.
A subagent could not edit the shared checkout's plan file, so PR status was not recorded in NEXT-WORK.md.
Several CI runs failed on lints, a stray blank line, or tests that assumed the old behavior, requiring reruns.
Push of the redesign to #330 was rejected as non-fast-forward and needed a rebase.
Benchmark timings were noisy because another process was compiling on the machine.
The first gix spike was unfair (unused diff resource cache) and the user had to point out the missed optimization.
The first profile was incomplete and misleading, and it exposed quadratic aggregation in newly written code.
